issues.legal_issue: A revenue right retained by former rulers who had become subjects may constitute an implied assignment of land revenue.
material_facts: The holders had originally ruled the territories they occupied, but governmental powers were progressively removed from them.
By the time revenue settlements were made, the British Government exercised sovereign powers and the holders had been reduced to subjects with certain privileges.
The British Government took over the settlement and collection of revenue and paid the holders a share of the collections.
There was no express grant of the revenue right.
issues.conclusion: The holders’ right to receive the land revenue rested on an implied grant and amounted to an assignment of land revenue within the statutory definition of a jagir.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(1)(a) of the Punjab Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1957 covers assignments of land revenue. A grant may be implied, and a person’s status is either sovereign or subject, not an intermediate status; once former rulers have become subjects, their revenue rights may be held under an implied grant. The Court relied on Thakur Amar Singhji v. State of Rajasthan, [1955] 2 S.C.R. 303. It also applied the principle that sovereignty can be acquired otherwise than by conquest, relying on Cook v. Sir James Gordon Sprigg, (1899) A.C. 572; Vajesingji Joravar Singji v. Secretary of State, [1924] L.R. 51 I.A. 357; M/s. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, [1959] S.C.R. 729; and Promod Chandra Deb v. State of Orissa.

predicates.revenue_resumption_challenge: A proceeding challenges the resumption of a right to receive land revenue.
predicates.former_rulers_lost_sovereign_powers: The holders had formerly exercised governmental powers but were later reduced to subjects.
predicates.government_controlled_revenue_and_paid_s: The government took control of revenue settlement or collection and paid the holders a share of the revenue.

issues.definition: When a resumption challenge concerns former rulers who became subjects and a government controlled the revenue and paid them a share, their revenue right is treated as an implied assignment.

issues.legal_issue: A historical assignment made by a predecessor government may qualify as an assignment made by the State Government when the governing definition includes predecessor governments retrospectively.
material_facts: The asserted implied grant arose from the British Government’s control of revenue and payment of a share to the holders.
The amended statutory definition of State Government included predecessor governments and was given retrospective effect from the commencement of the principal Act.
The amendment was challenged as outside the State Legislature’s competence.
issues.conclusion: The British Government fell within the statutory definition of State Government, and the retrospective amendment applied to the grants in question.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(1)(a) and 2(5) of the Punjab Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1957, read with section 1(2) of the Punjab Resumption of Jagirs (Amendment) Act, 1959, make the definition include predecessor governments and give the amendment retrospective operation. The Court held that the definition was wide enough to include the government that made the grant.

predicates.resumption_challenge: A proceeding challenges the resumption of a historical revenue grant.
predicates.historic_grant_made_by_predecessor_autho: The government that made the historical grant preceded the government currently responsible for the territory.
predicates.definition_includes_predecessor_authorit: The governing definition includes predecessor governments and applies that inclusion to the relevant earlier period.

issues.definition: In a resumption challenge, a historical grant made by a predecessor authority counts as a State Government grant when the applicable definition includes predecessor authorities retrospectively.

issues.legal_issue: A State Legislature is competent to enact legislation resuming jagirs where the legislation concerns rights in land or land revenue.
material_facts: The legislation provided for resumption of jagirs consisting of rights to land revenue.
The challengers argued that the State Legislature lacked competence to enact the legislation and to amend its definition of State Government.
The subject matter concerned land, land tenure, and land revenue.
issues.conclusion: The legislation, including the amendment, was within the State Legislature’s competence under entries 18 and 45 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Entries 18 and 45 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution confer legislative competence over land and land revenue, including land rights and the collection or alienation of revenue. The Court held that resumption of jagirs concerning land revenue falls within those subjects and that an amendment concerning the same subject matter is likewise within competence.

predicates.challenge_to_resumption_law: A proceeding challenges the validity of legislation providing for resumption of jagirs.
predicates.law_resumes_land_or_revenue_rights: The legislation concerns rights in land, land tenure, or land revenue.

issues.definition: A State Legislature has competence to enact a resumption law when the challenged law concerns rights in land or land revenue.

issues.legal_issue: A proceeding challenging the validity and application of a resumption law is not the proper scope for adjudicating a separate claim to compensation between an affected holder and a person asserting a reversionary interest.
material_facts: The matter before the Court concerned appeals from dismissal of writ petitions challenging the validity and application of the resumption legislation.
An intervener asserted a reversionary interest in the compensation payable for resumed property and requested directions to protect that interest.
Determining entitlement to the compensation would require adjudication of competing rights, which was outside the scope of the proceedings before the Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to decide the competing compensation claims or issue directions concerning payment, leaving the claimant to pursue an appropriate separate proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the limited scope of an appeal concerning dismissal of a writ petition challenging the validity and application of the resumption legislation. It distinguished Satinder Singh v. Umrao Singh, A.I.R. 1961 S.C. 908, which involved compensation under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and relied on State of Orissa v. Madan Gopal Rungta, [1952] S.C.R. 28, in declining to grant relief that did not follow from determination of the rights properly before it.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal_on_resumption: The proceeding is an appeal from dismissal of a writ petition challenging a resumption law.
predicates.intervener_claims_competing_compensation: A person intervening in the proceeding asserts an interest in compensation payable to another claimant.
predicates.compensation_entitlement_requires_separa: Deciding the asserted interest would require adjudication of competing entitlement to compensation beyond the issues in the proceeding.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerning a resumption-law challenge includes a competing compensation claim that requires separate adjudication, compensation entitlement is not determined in that proceeding.
